corrections.how: Phase 1, Tony's phone only. App Store OpenClaw app reaching the gateway over the tailnet. Pairing code from `openclaw qr --limited`: this drops only operator.admin, and the phone still holds operator.write, operator.approvals and operator.talk.secrets. Leave the phone's node surface unapproved, or deny its commands with `gateway.nodes.commands.deny`, so pairing adds voice and nothing else. The app is a gateway client first. Every pairing profile includes operator.read, which covers session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace; the app's Agents > Files screen and its offline transcript cache show exactly that. On a second adult's phone this means the other adult's agent memory is readable.
The default pairing code includes the admin scope, and in every profile the app lets its user pick any agent.

`--limited` removes only operator.admin. The phone keeps operator.write (chat with any agent, gateway-wide tool invocation, node command relay) and operator.approvals, so a second phone is also a second approver for every pending request.
`--voice-node` does not rescue the native loop: the chat turn is chat.send, which the docs class as write-scoped, and that profile holds only read and talk.

Pairing registers the phone as the gateway's first node. Once a node surface is approved, the default iOS policy allows location, contacts search, calendar events, reminders and latest photos to any write-scoped client, subject to the iOS permission on the phone.
App Store builds register with a vendor-hosted push relay: a new third-party dependency and egress destination for this gateway.

Talk playback uses the Talk speech provider, not the general tts block. The docs name elevenlabs (cloud), mlx and system for Talk, and the mlx helper ships with the Mac app, which is not installed here; expect the iPhone's own system voice.
A lost or unlocked phone is now a gateway credential rather than just an iMessage sender; Tony needs the device-revocation step written down before pairing.

corrections.description: One reviewed set of limits that goes in before any voice surface is switched on: voice-only devices get a read-plus-talk credential, Talk has an explicit default owner, realtime voice must confirm aloud before acting, cloud speech providers are switched off in config rather than by instruction, and a house rule says shared-room microphones never reach a memory-holding or cloud-backed agent while kids are around. It narrows what a voice device can do; it does not stop a paired device from reading both adults' agents.
corrections.how: Pair voice-only devices (a Watch, a room device) with `openclaw qr --voice-node`: node token plus only operator.read and operator.talk. Do not treat `--limited` as a voice profile; it removes only operator.admin and keeps write, approvals and talk.secrets. Set `talk.agentId` explicitly, because a multi-agent gateway has no unambiguous Talk owner. Use `talk.realtime.brain: agent-consult` and keep the built-in spoken-confirmation gate, knowing it applies to voice-originated realtime consult runs; the native speech loop is ordinary chat and relies on the existing hooks and approvals. Shut the cloud-speech doors in config: leave `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off, set `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false`, configure no cloud speech keys, and block the speech hosts at the egress proxy, because any authorized sender can run `/tts provider <id>`. Keep voice devices' node surfaces unapproved or denied with `gateway.nodes.commands.deny`. Add a read-only listing of paired devices, their scopes and their node commands to the operator's inspect script. Per-person enforcement would need `gateway.roles` on top of a verified identity per person; that is a separate project and unproven with the mobile apps.
caveats: operator.read is broad and is in every pairing profile: session lists, chat history, logs and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace. There is no voice credential today that cannot read both adults' agent memory.
A read-plus-talk device probably cannot run the native speech loop, because the chat turn is write-scoped. Least privilege therefore pushes voice devices onto the realtime path, which is cloud audio.
Talk clients choose the agent (the Watch literally asks which agent), so 'Jordan's device only reaches jordan-main' is not enforced without gateway roles.

There is no speaker identification anywhere in the stack. Whoever is near the microphone is the user, and the spoken yes can come from anyone in the room; the FaceTime doc says the same about its own calls.

With roles configured, plain device or bootstrap tokens are rejected for operator connections, so roles change how every app signs in and need a verified identity per person. The docs add that the write scope stays gateway-wide even under roles.
Standalone Watch setup needs the iPhone connected with operator.admin, which conflicts with pairing phones below admin.
corrections.safety: This entry is the control layer for the voice lens: credential scopes, tool policy, provider switches in config and a host-enforced confirmation are limits the model cannot talk its way past. What it cannot deliver is the section 1b separation between the two adults on app or voice devices, or the kids rule; those need verified role enforcement and a local model, neither of which exists yet. Until then the only compliant voice device is the operator's own.

corrections.name: Local neural voice for spoken replies (local-only once cloud speech is switched off)
corrections.how: Gateway `tts` block. Documented option A: Speech Swift's local server on loopback (`brew install speech`, `speech-server --port 8080`) with the `openai` speech provider pointed at the loopback base URL, `model` tts-1 (which selects Kokoro) and `responseFormat` wav. Option B: `tts-local-cli` running the `speech` or `say` command. Option C: the bundled sherpa-onnx-tts skill with a Piper voice. Per-agent control through `agents.entries.<id>.tts` (off for research and inbox). `tts.auto: inbound` gives a voice answer to a voice memo; `/tts latest` reads the previous reply. ffmpeg on the host for conversions. To make local-only true rather than assumed: set `tts.provider` explicitly, set `tts.providers.microsoft.enabled: false`, configure no cloud speech keys, keep `tts.modelOverrides.allowProvider` off, and block the cloud speech hosts at the egress proxy. For anything a child will hear, also turn the summary step off or point `tts.summaryModel` at a local model. Option C is only usable as a `tts-local-cli` command here: the bundled skill is run by an agent through exec, which no agent has.
caveats: iMessage is not a voice-note channel: the reply is an audio file attachment, not a voice bubble. The voice-bubble option (`asVoice` on upload-file) belongs to the Private API action set, which needs SIP off.
Local engines emit WAV, so a few minutes of speech is several megabytes.
Long replies are summarized by the chat model before synthesis (a cloud call) or truncated.
Two tempting shortcuts are cloud services and must stay off for kids' content: the no-key Microsoft provider (Edge online TTS) and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs).
The built-in `tts` tool only speaks when asked, which is the right default: nobody wants every text reply doubled as audio.

Local-only is not the default. The keyless Microsoft provider is enabled by default, and the docs say other configured providers act as fallbacks, so a stopped local server could end in a cloud call unless Microsoft is disabled.

`/tts provider <id>` is open to any authorized sender and writes one preference file on the gateway host, so a single text can move speech to another provider for everyone. Having no cloud provider configured is the control; a prompt rule is not.

Option A adds a third-party Homebrew package and a long-running loopback server under the happy user, plus a model download: an install, a launch agent, a firewall rule and a one-time egress exception.
corrections.safety: Speech synthesis is an output transformation on the gateway host and adds no new way for an agent to send data out. It is local-only, and so usable for kids' content later, only after the cloud speech providers are disabled in config and blocked at the proxy; the default provider chain and the provider slash command would otherwise allow a cloud voice. Long replies pass through a summary model before synthesis, which must be local or off for kids. Keep provider switching by directive off (VOX-03).
unverified: Kokoro or Piper voice quality and speed on this Mac.
Whether pointing `tts.providers.openai` at loopback has any side effect on the earlier decision not to add a catalog openai model provider (it is a different config block).
Whether scheduled announce deliveries (briefs) pass through Auto-TTS or only interactive replies do.
Whether the fallback chain actually reaches the Microsoft online voice when the selected local provider errors.
Which hosts the Speech Swift package contacts to download its models.

corrections.how:
Trigger is deterministic, not a model decision: a `before_dispatch` claim on a fixed prefix such as `announce:` from an adult's handle hands the parent's words verbatim to the tool, so

-main (which reads search results) never decides to speak to the house and no cloud-written text is played to the children. If an agent tool form is kept, each announcement needs an approval. The tool itself, `announce(text, rooms)`, lives in the planned `home-sonos` plugin. It synthesizes the text with the local engine from VOX-04, serves the file from a small HTTP server bound to the LAN address only (one directory, short-lived random file names, inbound firewall exception for the speakers), and plays it. Route A, no Home Assistant: the Sonos audio-clip command `loadAudioClip` with a `streamUrl`, which mixes the clip with whatever is playing but is documented under the cloud Control API with OAuth and an API key; or sonoscli `play-uri`, which replaces what is playing and restores nothing. Route B, if Home Assistant is ever installed for VOX-11: its Sonos integration plays an announcement with `announce: true` and restores the volume. In code: text length cap, volume cap, quiet hours from G001, speaker allowlist, a daily cap.
caveats: The bundled sonoscli skill documents discover, status, play, volume and grouping only; it has no announce or speech command. The tool's site lists `play-url` and `play-uri`, but I could not confirm that either resumes the previous music.
Sonos audio clips only work on players that report the AUDIO_CLIP capability; the two speakers here are unchecked.
LAN speaker control from the gateway needs the macOS Local Network permission for the launchd node process.
A talking house at the wrong moment is worse than no feature; quiet hours and a low daily cap matter more than voice quality.

The overlay is unverified without Home Assistant. Sonos documents loadAudioClip under its cloud Control API (OAuth scope plus API key), and Home Assistant's page says its announcements need TCP port 1443 open on each speaker, which suggests a local interface exists; Sonos' own page does not document one.
Home Assistant's page warns that older hardware and S1 firmware may not fully support announcements.
The 9 Oct scan found the two speakers in the living room and the family room, so an announcement does not reach the kitchen or bedrooms.
The clip server would be the first LAN-facing listener on the gateway Mac.
The Sonos cloud route puts a Sonos account token on the gateway and makes a house announcement depend on an internet round trip.
corrections.safety:
The audience is everyone in the house, guests and children included, so this is an outbound channel in its own right even though nothing leaves the building. It must not be callable by an agent that reads untrusted content without an approval:

-main reads search and research results, so the safe trigger is a fixed prefix claimed before the model, speaking the parent's words verbatim. Never reachable from research or mail readers. Speech is synthesized locally, with the VOX-04 hardening in place. Text length, volume, quiet hours, speaker allowlist and a daily cap are enforced in code. No lock, alarm or door is involved.

caveats: iOS voice features are best-effort unless the app stays in the foreground, hence Guided Access plus keep-awake. Months of always-on use on a charger is untested.
On iOS the speech recognizer may use Apple's network service, and the docs only promise the on-device-only wake contract for macOS.
Kids will talk to it. Every agent today is cloud-backed, so under the family's own rule this terminal is for parents only until a local model exists. Guided Access controls taps, not voices.
No speaker identification: a guest can ask anything the kitchen agent can answer, so keep memory and private data out of that agent.

A talk-only device is not a blind device. operator.read covers session lists, chat history and read-only browsing of every agent's workspace, and the app has Sessions and Agents > Files screens plus an offline transcript cache. Guided Access keeps people inside the app, not out of those screens; disabling touch regions is a brittle workaround.

The native speech loop sends its turn with a write-scoped method, so a voice-node pairing probably supports only the realtime path: kitchen audio, children included, streamed to a cloud voice model. Pairing with --limited instead would put write and approval rights on a counter-top device.
The phone also registers as a node with camera, screen and location command families; an always-on device in the kitchen needs its node surface left unapproved or denied at the gateway.

Holding the device to the kitchen agent rests on `talk.agentId` (one gateway-wide default) or on the app's own agent picker. Hard enforcement would need gateway roles, which reject the bootstrap token this pairing uses.
If Tony also wants an idle iPhone as a device for Happy to operate, that is a different job; a phone pinned by Guided Access cannot be both.
corrections.safety: No safe placement exists today. The credential cannot send messages or change config, but it can read both parents' agents; the room is shared with children and every model is cloud-backed; and nothing a curious child or a guest cannot get around holds the device to a stateless agent. Revisit when there is a local model (M2), a verified way to restrict a device to one agent with no cross-agent read, and a local speech path that works with a talk-only credential.
